Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 78, verses 6–16:

[[Mahmud said: "If you ask: how is His saying ﴿Have We not made the earth a cradle?﴾ connected to what precedes it? ... etc." Ahmad said: His first answer is sound, but the second is not correct, for it is built on the crooked doctrine that it is obligatory to consider what is good and what is best (al-salah wal-aslah, meaning what is best for the servant), and on the belief that reward and punishment are obligatory for God by reason, according to the requirement of divine wisdom. He has already finished refuting this principle.]]

I say: When they denied the resurrection, it was said to them: Did not the One to whom the resurrection is attributed create these wondrous creatures, which indicate the perfection of power? So what is the basis for denying His power to resurrect, when resurrection is nothing but an origination like these originations? Or it was said to them: Did He not perform these many actions? And the Wise does not perform any action in vain, while what you deny of resurrection and recompense leads to the conclusion that He is futile in everything He does.

﴿Have We not made the earth a cradle?﴾ (mihadan) means a bed or resting place. It is also read mahdan. Its meaning is that it is for them like a cradle for a child, which is what is spread out for him so that he sleeps upon it, the noun being used for the thing made to be spread out, as in "the prince's striking" (darb al-amir). Or it is an attribute given by the verbal noun. Or it means "possessor of a cradle," that is, We set it firm with mountains, as a tent is fixed with pegs.

Sabatan means death. The one who is put to sleep (al-masbut) is the dead one, from al-sabt, which means cutting off, because he is cut off from movement. Sleep is one of the two kinds of death, and it is built on the pattern of ailments.

Since He made sleep a death, He made waking a livelihood, meaning a life, in His saying ﴿and made the day for livelihood﴾, that is, a time of livelihood in which you awaken and move about in your needs and earnings. It is said that sabat means rest. ﴿And made the night a garment﴾ covers you from eyes when you want to flee from an enemy or to raid him by night, or to conceal what you do not want to be seen of many matters.

Abu al-Tayyib (al-Mutanabbi) said:

How many a favor the darkness of night has shown you,
which proves that the Manichaeans are lying!

And protected you from the harm of enemies, as you journeyed toward them by night,
and the one of pampered reserve (the beloved, veiled) visited you in it.

Kam (how many) here is a word of multiplicity. Yad (favor) means a blessing. Takhbir (proves) means indicates by a metonymic figure. The Manichaeans are a sect that attributes good to the Light and evil to the Darkness. So he refuted them in the first line, argued for it, and built the notion of favor in the second. Al-dalal means withholding from the veiled one while being pleased with him. Tasra is a circumstantial clause, and al-muhajjab is an adjective of dhu al-dalal. This clarifies the Manichaean question: no one disagreed that God is one except the dualists. They said: you find in the world much good and much evil, and the one cannot be both good and evil, so each of good and evil has an independent agent. The Manichaeans and the Daysaniyya, who are among the dualists, said: the agent of good is the Light, and the agent of evil is the Darkness, and they asserted that these two are eternal, sensing, hearing, seeing bodies. The Magians, who are also among the dualists, said: the agent of good is Yazdan, and the agent of evil is Ahriman, meaning the Devil. All of this is clearly false.

﴿Seven heavens, strong﴾ (sab'an shidadan): shidad is the plural of shadida, meaning firm and strong in creation, which the passing of ages does not affect.

﴿A blazing lamp﴾ (wahhajan): shining and burning, meaning the sun. "The fire blazed" (tawahhajat al-nar) means it flared up. The sun blazes with its light and its heat.

﴿The rain-bearing clouds﴾ (al-mu'sirat): the clouds when they are about to be squeezed by the winds so that they rain, as you say "reap the crop" when it is time to reap it. From this is "the girl has reached maturity" (a'sarat al-jariya) when she approaches menstruation.

Ikrima read bi-l-mu'sirat ("from the squeezing ones"), and there are two interpretations: that the intended ones are the winds which are about to squeeze the clouds, or that the intended ones are the clouds, because when the descent is from them, it is attributed to them, as you say "he gave with his hand a dirham" and "he gave by his hand." It is reported from Mujahid that al-mu'sirat are the winds with whirlwinds. It is reported from al-Hasan and Qatada that they are the heavens. Its interpretation is that the water descends from the sky to the clouds, so it is as if the heavens are squeezed, that is, they are moved to squeeze and are enabled to do so.

If you ask: what is the reasoning of the one who reads min al-mu'sirat and interprets them as the winds with whirlwinds, while rain does not descend from winds? I say: the winds are what produce the clouds and milk their udders. The udder (khalf) is the teat of a she-camel, as the Sihah indicates. So it is correct to make the winds the origin of the descent. It has been reported that God sends winds which carry water from the sky to the clouds. If that is correct, then the descent from them is clear.

If you ask: Ibn Kaysan mentioned that he took al-mu'sirat to mean al-mughithat (those who give relief), and the one who squeezes is the one who gives relief, not the one who is squeezed. It is said: "he squeezed it, so it was squeezed out" (a'tasara). I say: its reasoning is that they are those who are about to be squeezed, meaning it is time for them to be squeezed, that is, to give relief, pouring forth abundantly. It is said: "he poured it and poured himself out." In a hadith: "The best pilgrimage is al-'ajj and al-thajj." [The Tirmidhi transmitted it from a hadith of Ibn Umar with a similar meaning and weakened it, Ibrahim ibn Yazid al-Kharizi. He and Ibn Majah transmitted it from the narration of Muhammad ibn al-Mankadir, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Yarbu', from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, similarly raised to the Prophet. He said: Ibn al-Mankadir did not hear from Abd al-Rahman ibn Yarbu'.] Al-'ajj means raising the voice with the talbiyah, and al-thajj means pouring out the blood of the sacrificial animal. Ibn Abbas was one who poured out (mathajjan) and let flow (yusbil ghirban), meaning he poured out words in his sermon. Al-A'raj read thajjajan. Mathajij al-ma' means its pouring, and the water gushes into the valley.

﴿Grain and plants﴾ (habban wa nabatan) means what is used for food from wheat and barley, and what is fed as fodder from straw and grass, as He said ﴿Eat, and let your cattle graze﴾, and ﴿the grain with its husk and the fragrant herbs﴾.

﴿Luxuriant gardens﴾ (alfafan): intertwined, and it has no singular, like al-awza' and al-akhyaf. It is said its singular is laff. Al-Sahib, the author of al-Iqlid, said: al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Tusi recited to me:

A garden thickly intertwined, and a life overflowing,
and companions, all of them white and radiant.

Laff (with a kasra) is what is intertwined, meant as the intertwined garden because of the density of its trees and leaves. Mughdiq means abundant and wide. Bid (white) is a metaphor for good reports, and it may be taken literally. Azhar means one with a bright face, so zahr means those with bright faces, like ahmar and hamr, meaning his companions are noble of character, or white and handsome of face. The regular pattern for the plural of af'al and fa'la' is fa'l with a sukun on the middle letter. In poetry it is permissible to vowel it when its middle and final letters are sound and not doubled, as here and as in his saying:

And the dark-eyed ones have denied me, the ones with the wide eyes.

It is permissible for the poet to move a sukun by the vowel of what precedes it for the meter, and it is permissible to move it by the vowel of what follows it when it is at pause, so that it becomes with a fatha on the ha', like ghurfa and ghuraf.

Ibn Qutayba claimed that it is lafa'
and laff, then alfaf. I do not think he found an analogue to it, like khadr and akhdar, hamr and ahmar. If it were said that it is the plural of multafifa (intertwined), with the extra letters removed, it would be a reasonable opinion.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 78, verse 31–36:

*Mafāzan* (a place of success): success and attainment of the desired goal. Or it means a place of success. It was also said: deliverance from what is therein (the Fire). Or it means a place of deliverance. *Mafāz* is explained by what follows it.

*Ḥadā'iq* (gardens): orchards containing various kinds of fruit-bearing trees. *A'nāb* (grapes): vines.

*Kawā'ib* (maidens with rounded breasts): those whose breasts have become firm and round [[His saying "fallakat thadyahunna" (whose breasts have risen round): in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, "falaka thady al-jāriya taflīkan" (the girl's breast became round), and tafalluk means to become round. (ʿ)]], and they are *nawāhid* (rising-breasted). *Atrāb* (of equal age). *Lidāt* (companions).

*Daqāq* (overflowing): *mutraʿa* (brimming). *Adhqa al-ḥawḍ* means he filled the basin until it said, "Enough!"

It was recited: "Lord of the heavens" (rabb al-samawat). "Al-Rahman" is read in the nominative (bil-raf'), meaning: "He is the Lord of the heavens, al-Rahman." Or, "Lord of the heavens" is the subject (mubtada'), "al-Rahman" is its attribute (sifah), and "la yamlikun" is the predicate (khabar). Or both are predicates (khabarani). It is also read in the genitive (bil-jarr) as an apposition (badal) from "rabbika," and with the first in the genitive and the second in the nominative as a subject whose predicate is "la yamlikun." Or it is "Huwa al-Rahman, la yamlikun."

The pronoun in "la yamlikun" refers to the people of the heavens and the earth. That is: nothing in their hands of the address (khitab) that Allah addresses and commands concerning reward and punishment is a single address that they could dispose of as owners do, adding to it or subtracting from it. Or: they do not have the power to address Him with anything about reducing the punishment or increasing the reward, except that He grants it to them and permits them to do so. "Yawma yaqumu" is related to "la yamlikun," or to "la yatakallamun."

The meaning is: those who are the most excellent of creation (in the Mu'tazilah view, this includes their preference over humans; the view of Ahl al-Sunnah, the People of the Sunnah, is the preference of humans over them. Apparently the Spirit is like the angel in this dispute, so reflect on this. (ʿA)), the most noble of them, the most obedient of them and the closest to Him, namely the Spirit and the angels, cannot speak in His presence. So what do you think of those other than them among the people of the heavens and the earth?

The Spirit (al-Ruh) is greater in creation than the angels, more noble than them, and closer to the Lord of the worlds. It was said: it is a great angel, and Allah has not created after the Throne a creation greater than him. It was said: they are not the angels, and they eat. It was said: Jibril.

There are two conditions: that the speaker is permitted to speak, and that he speaks what is right, so he does not intercede for anyone except one who is approved (murtada). (Mahmud said: "The restriction of intercession to two conditions..." Ahmad [Ibn al-Munayyir] said: he alludes that intercession does not benefit those who commit major sins among the monotheists, and he stated this explicitly in places mentioned earlier, deriving it from the claim that intercession is specific to those who are approved, and those with major sins are not approved. Thus he erred, for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, did not single them out with faith and monotheism and cause them to die upon it unless He had approved them for that, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿And He does not approve for His servants disbelief; but if you are grateful, He approves it for you﴾ [39:7]. So He made gratitude, meaning faith as opposed to disbelief, approved by Allah, and its possessor approved.) For His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they do not intercede except for those whom He approves﴾ [21:28].

**Surah 78, verse 40, from al-Zamakhshari's al-Kashshaf:**

"Al-mar'" (the man): it refers to the disbeliever, according to the saying of the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, We have warned you of a near punishment﴾.

"Al-kafir" (the disbeliever) is an apparent noun placed in the position of a pronoun, to increase the condemnation. The meaning is ﴿what his hands have sent forth﴾ of evil, like the saying ﴿Taste the punishment of the burning. This is for what your hands have sent forth﴾, and ﴿We will make him taste the punishment of the burning on the Day of Resurrection. [It will be said], "This is for what your hands have sent forth"﴾, and ﴿for what their hands have sent forth. And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾.

"Ma" (what) may be interrogative, in the accusative governed by "qaddamat" (sent forth), meaning: he looks at what his hands have sent forth. It may also be relative, in the accusative governed by "yanzuru" (looks), as in the expression "nazartuhu" meaning "I looked at him" (nazartu ilayhi). The returning pronoun in the relative clause is omitted.

It was said: "al-mar'" is general, and the disbeliever is specified from it.

It is narrated from Qatadah that it refers to the believer.

"Ya laytani kuntu turaban" (Would that I had been dust): in the world, so that I had not been created and not been made responsible; or, would that I were dust on this Day, so that I had not been resurrected.

It was said: Allah gathers the animals, which are not responsible, so that retribution is taken for the hornless (animal) from the horned, then He returns them to dust, and the disbeliever wishes for their state.

It was said: the disbeliever is Iblis, who sees Adam and his offspring and their rewards, so he wishes that he were the thing he despised when he said ﴿You created me from fire and You created him from clay﴾.

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites the surah 'Amma yatasa'alun' (Surah An-Naba'), Allah will give him to drink of the coolness of the drink on the Day of Resurrection."
